title: Circular Motion Needs a Force Pulling Inward
hook: Anything moving in a circle is accelerating, even at constant speed — so something must constantly pull it inward. There is no real outward force flinging you out.
key_points: Moving in a circle constantly changes direction, which counts as acceleration.
That acceleration requires a net inward (centripetal) force toward the center.
The force can be gravity, tension, friction, or a wall pushing in.
There's no real centrifugal force; the outward feeling is inertia going straight.
content_html: When something moves in a circle, its direction is always changing — and a change in velocity is acceleration, even if the speed never changes. By Newton's second law, acceleration needs a force, so circular motion always requires a net force pointed toward the center of the circle. That inward force is called centripetal force.
extra_html: The centripetal force isn't a new kind of force; it's whatever happens to be pulling inward in a given situation. For a ball on a string it's the tension; for a car rounding a bend it's friction between tires and road; for the Moon it's gravity. The familiar outward push you feel in a sharp turn is not a real force pulling you out — it's your own inertia trying to carry you in a straight line while the vehicle curves into you. Cut the string or hit a patch of ice, and the object flies off tangent to the circle, not radially outward. Wikipedia lays out the geometry and why "centrifugal force" is best understood as inertia.

flashcards.prompt: Why does an object moving at constant speed in a circle still accelerate?
flashcards.back_html: Because its direction is constantly changing, and any change in velocity — including direction — is acceleration. That demands a net inward force.

flashcards.prompt: What keeps a car moving around a flat curve?

choices.text: Friction between the tires and road, pointing inward (centripetal)
An outward centrifugal force pushing the car around
The car's own inertia curving the path

flashcards.explanation_html: A centripetal force — here, tire friction pointing toward the center — bends the car's path into a circle. On ice with no friction, it slides straight.

flashcards.prompt: What is the 'centrifugal force' you feel pushed outward in a turning car?

choices.text: Not a real force — it's your inertia trying to keep going straight
A real outward force created by the circular motion
The reaction force from the centripetal force

flashcards.explanation_html: Your body wants to travel in a straight line; the car turns into you, so it feels like you're flung outward. The only real force here points inward.
